name: Combustion analysers and handheld CO meters
summary: Heating technicians' handheld meters that pump flue gas or room air past gas sensors and show CO in ppm and O2 in %, with CO2 and efficiency calculated.
uses: Measures CO in ppm and O2 in %, plus stack and air temperature; CO2, air-free CO, excess air and efficiency are calculated (Bacharach InTech)
Made for tuning burners and checking flue gas on furnaces, boilers and gas water heaters; some also read CO in room air (testo 310; Bacharach InTech)
Not an alarm: testo says the 310 must not be used as a safety (alarm) device (testo 310)
Zeroes its sensors at switch-on, so the probe must be in open, CO-free air then or the zero is wrong; testo flags a bad zero as an error (testo 310)
Tops out at 2,000–4,000 ppm CO; the InTech's CO protect feature cuts in above range, and testo says purge the cell in fresh air (Bacharach InTech; testo 310)
Cigarette smoke adds over 50 ppm to a room reading; solvent, degreaser and formaldehyde vapours can damage the cells (testo 310)
identify: A handheld meter on a hose with a metal probe that goes into the flue; the hose has a water trap and filter (Bacharach InTech; testo 310). The screen shows O2 %, CO ppm, CO2 %, efficiency and flue and air temperatures, and you choose the fuel: natural gas, oil, kerosene or propane (Bacharach InTech). Common makes: the Bacharach Fyrite InTech reads 0–2,000 ppm CO, runs on four AA cells and carries EN 50379 and CE marks (Bacharach InTech); the testo 310 reads 0–4,000 ppm CO, has a rechargeable pack and an ambient CO mode for room air (testo 310). Air-free CO is a calculated flue figure, not what you are breathing (Bacharach InTech). Room-air limits for scale: NIOSH recommends no more than 35 ppm averaged over a work shift and never above 200 ppm, and treats 1,200 ppm as immediately dangerous to life (NIOSH CO); CCOHS gives the ACGIH limit as 25 ppm (CCOHS CO). The testo 310 is made to work only from -5 to 45 °C (testo 310).
test: 1. Power: the InTech runs at least 20 hours on four AA cells (Bacharach InTech); the testo 310's pack only charges at 0–35 °C (testo 310). 2. Switch on outdoors, in clean air, with the probe out of any flue: it zeroes its sensors (testo 310). After that, with no error code showing, O2 should read about 20.9 %, the fresh-air figure and the top of the InTech's O2 range (Bacharach InTech), and CO about 0, within the testo 310's ±0.2 vol.% O2 and ±20 ppm CO (testo 310). 3. Error messages: on the testo 310, E04 means a worn O2 cell and E07 a worn CO cell, and the manual says to replace the cell and calibrate. E06 (O2 cell near its wear limit, or not in fresh air at zeroing), E12 (CO baseline up by over 50 ppm) and E13 (CO baseline unstable) may only be a poor zero: redo the zeroing in clean air, and if the message stays, replace the cell (testo 310). 4. Age: makers warrant standard O2 and CO cells for 2 years; testo's Longlife cells are rated up to 6 years with heavy use (Bacharach InTech; testo 300). 5. No safe home check shows the CO cell still responds. Testo lists cigarette smoke only as something that skews an ambient CO reading by over 50 ppm (testo 310), not as a test, so don't blow smoke or exhaust at the probe. A 0 in clean air straight after zeroing doesn't show the cell still senses CO: treat a meter of unknown age or calibration as a rough guide. 6. Empty the water trap with the pump off and check the filter; condensate in the gas path damages the cells. Never open a cell: it holds acid that can burn (testo 310).

decay.note: Estimate. O2 and CO cells are warranted for 2 years, Longlife ones rated up to 6 (Bacharach InTech; testo 300); rechargeable packs die if left flat, and filters and water traps need spares.

improvise: For a sleeping area, a home CO alarm is the right tool: it is built to sound on its own, and these meters are not (testo 310; First Alert CO710). A multi-gas monitor with a CO sensor also alarms. Without any meter, judge burners by eye: a yellow flame means fuel isn't burning completely and CO may be present (First Alert CO710), but flame colour can't clear a burner, since a cracked heat exchanger or a blocked flue can also put CO in the house (First Alert CO710). Check chimneys and flues for nests, debris, rust and cracks, look for backdraft at the draft hood of a running furnace, and check for cracks in the furnace heat exchanger (First Alert CO710). Your nose is useless: CO can't be seen or smelled (Intertek CSA 6.19). Headache, tiredness, dizziness or nausea in anyone near a burner means get everyone outside (Intertek CSA 6.19).
